Coverage

Facilities that have submitted, by provinceFacilities

Facility counts sum cleanly to the total - no facility appears in two provinces. Submissions are NOT comparable across provinces: East and West are inflated by the three one-medicine-per-submission facilities. Medicine observations are the comparable column, and they are far more even (387/331/326/207/108) than the submission counts suggest.

Coverage is even: every facility carries 42-56 medicine observations, and each province covers all 55 medicines. The wide spread in submission counts is purely data-entry style - the three one-medicine-per-submission facilities still ended up assessing the full instrument. Facility-level rates are therefore comparable.

12 duplicate row(s) removed of 14,390 facility x medicine observations. The pair is the unit of analysis, so a duplicate double-counts the observation. The rule keeps the row carrying an actual assessment, then the later submission; it is applied in the analysis, not in the export, because the export is rebuilt from both servers on every fetch. 7 of them DISAGREE with the row kept - the rule picked one, but only the collector can say which visit was right, so those medicines should be confirmed before they are reported on.

EastKibungo CSMUTUNZI Yves### Key Findings * **Beclomethasone:** Mutuelle is not reimbursing beclomethasone at Kibungo Health Centre. Salbutamol has been used as an alternative where appropriate. * **Gliclazide 60 mg tablets:** Mutuelle has not been reimbursing gliclazide at Kibungo Health Centre since **May 2025**. Metformin is being considered as an alternative, or patients may be referred to the hospital when necessary. The RMS is already aware of the issue and advised the Health Centre to procure the medicine while engaging Mutuelle to address the reimbursement issue. * **Diclofenac suppositories:** A similar reimbursement issue has been reported for diclofenac suppositories, and the issue has persisted for approximately **one year** without resolution. * **Medicine ordering when RMS stock is unavailable:** The Health Centre does not consistently place orders when the RMS system indicates that a medicine is unavailable. This may prevent the RMS from having visibility of the facility's ongoing demand and urgency for the product. The stock manager should continue submitting requests for needed medicines even when the RMS status indicates that the product is unavailable. This will help the RMS identify unmet demand and prioritize replenishment when stock becomes available. * **Repeated requests for unfilled medicines:** There is a tendency to stop requesting a medicine after an initial request is not fulfilled. Stock managers should regularly renew requests for medicines that remain needed, particularly when previous requests were not supplied, to ensure that the RMS remains aware of the continued demand. ### Recommendation For **non-moving medicines**, mechanisms should be explored to return or redistribute the stock to **Zipline or other health facilities/hospitals** where there is a demonstrated need, rather than allowing the medicines to expire. For example, **ethambutol** has reportedly remained non-moving at the facility for nearly two years, while the same medicine may be out of stock at other facilities. Redistribution should therefore be considered to reduce wastage and improve availability where the medicine is needed.

A similar situation was observed with Thiamine 100 mg, which was unavailable, while Thiamine 50 mg stock was presented. • Stock-on-hand verification: The total stock on hand was not fully counted because of the very large quantities involved. Instead, representative quantities of selected products were physically counted and compared with the stock recorded in the system. The quantities verified were consistent with the system records. • Stock levels: The facility generally maintains approximately 9 months of quantified/refill stock. The system warning level is set at 6 months, while the minimum stock level is approximately 4 months. • New medicine/protocol changes: When a new medicine or treatment protocol is introduced, RBC should inform CHUK and ensure that the facility receives the necessary information and training before implementation. For example, Abacavir/Lamivudine/Dolutegravir 60/30/5 mg (180 tablets) has been introduced as a new molecule, and appropriate communication and training should be provided. • RMS communication on stock deliveries:RMS should communicate clearly with CHUK regarding the reasons for delays or non-delivery of requested medicines, rather than providing only a general response without further explanation. SouthCyahinda CSUWAMBAJIMANA CharlesAssessment Findings: • Poor stock management practices were observed at the health facility. • Stock cards were missing for 12 managed commodities, including HIV Determine test kits, gloves, metformin, TB medicines, and other items. • Existing stock cards had no stock transaction records from January to June 2026. • Receipt and consumption of commodities could not be traced from the stock cards due to incomplete documentation. • Most internal requisition forms were unavailable, limiting verification of stock movements. • The e-LMIS is only used for submitting requisitions and is not utilized for routine stock management operations (receipts, issues, stock updates, or inventory management). Recommendation Update all stock cards using available source documents, including internal requisition forms, service consumption registers, delivery notes, expiry tracking lists, and any other valid stock records, to reconstruct and maintain accurate inventory records.

SouthKarama (Kamonyi) CSGaston KazenezaKey Issues and Recommendations RSSB reimbursement: Delays or non-reimbursement of certain medicines by RSSB are negatively affecting health facilities’ ability to pay for and requisition medicines from RMS. In particular, Diclofenac suppositories and Ringer’s Lactate are reportedly among the products that are frequently not reimbursed. This issue should be formally clarified and communicated to all relevant stakeholders. e-Ubuzima Pharmacy Desk training: RMS should provide targeted training to health facility pharmacy staff on the effective use of the e-Ubuzima Pharmacy Desk. Capturing consumption in e-Ubuzima: Currently, consumption in e-Ubuzima is primarily linked to individual patients. An additional consumption layer should be incorporated to capture the use of: Laboratory supplies and reagents; Medical products and supplies not directly dispensed to individual patients; and Other commodities consumed through service delivery or internal health facility operations. Cold chain infrastructure: The health facility requires a refrigerator to support the appropriate storage of temperature-sensitive products. The Ministry of Health may consider supporting the health centre through the provision of a refrigerator.

SouthNyamiyaga (Kamonyi) CSGaston KazenezaRecommendations 1. Rwanda Medical Supply (RMS) Expand the scope of ZIPLINE deliveries to cover a broader range of laboratory commodities and reagents, including pregnancy tests, HIV Determine tests, and haemoglobin testing supplies, to improve timely availability at health-facility level. 2. Ministry of Health (MoH) Strengthen staffing at health-facility level to support effective service delivery, with particular attention to ensuring that dedicated personnel are available to manage pharmaceutical and supply-chain activities. 3. Rwanda Social Security Board (RSSB) Review and clarify reimbursement arrangements for medicines reportedly not consistently reimbursed, including ciprofloxacin tablets, erythromycin tablets and syrup, diclofenac tablets, suppositories and injections. Strengthen engagement with health facilities to address reimbursement-related challenges and support uninterrupted service delivery, rather than creating additional operational constraints for facilities. 4. Health Facilities Strengthen stock-recording and inventory-management practices by ensuring that all available medicines and health commodities are supported by updated stock cards and are consistently recorded in e-Ubuzima. Ensure that dispensing registers are updated regularly and accurately to improve data completeness, traceability, stock visibility and the reliability of consumption data. Facilities were advised to address these gaps and reinforce compliance with established stock-management and reporting procedures.

Health posts with no entry in the Kobo facility list are captured under their parent health centre, and the field team says which submissions those are. Each correction is keyed by (facility as recorded, submission date) in FACILITY_OVERRIDES at the top of analyze_kobo_prescription.py, so it survives a re-fetch. Facility type is set to SGHP to match every other health post; district and sector are left as recorded, since a post sits inside its parent's catchment. Every other sheet in this workbook already reflects these changes.

Value-range flags

FlagRowsWhat it means
Available but quantity is zero37Answered 'available' then recorded 0 units - one of the two is wrong, and the row is classified from the quantity, so it reads as understock.
Months of stock above 1246Consumption near zero against a normal quantity. Real, but it distorts a mean - the profiles use the median throughout.
